title: Linux User Accounts
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Linux User Accounts and identify key concepts from the supplied syllabus.
Use an appropriate read-only check or controlled example to demonstrate linux user accounts.
Describe one common failure mode, safety consideration, or platform/version difference relevant to this topic.

content.intro: This lesson introduces linux user accounts as part of users, groups, permissions, and ownership. Begin with an observation you can safely repeat, then explain what the result tells you and what it does not prove.
content.why_it_matters: Explain account identity and permission checks, and manage access with least privilege in a test system.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Linux access decisions combine identity, ownership, mode bits, optional ACLs, and higher-level security policy. Apply least privilege.

content_blocks.execution_mode: manual-terminal; requires a local Linux environment or disposable VM; no isolated Linux runner is provided by CodeLeaf
content_blocks.expected_output: The current account name and numeric UID; values vary by environment.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a Linux machine, WSL environment, or disposable virtual machine. Check the command with its local manual page before adapting it. The in-page example shows reference output only; it does not execute Bash/Linux commands on the CodeLeaf server. Commands and output formats may vary by distribution and installed utility version.
content_blocks.reset_steps: These example commands are read-only or print-only. Exit the terminal when finished; if you adapt the task to create files, use a disposable practice folder and remove only the test files you deliberately created.
content_blocks.example_review_note: Topic-specific draft example authored for Linux course. Output is environment-dependent where stated; review on the target distribution before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First, state what you expect from the example. Run it in the intended environment, capture standard output and any error message, and inspect the exit status where meaningful. Then connect the observation to this lesson: Linux User Accounts. Do not infer more than the evidence supports.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake
content_blocks.text: A common mistake is to assume linux user accounts behaves identically on every distribution, kernel, utility version, and administrative policy. Verify the installed tool and consult the matching manual before using the procedure elsewhere.

content_blocks.title: Safety and compatibility
content_blocks.text: The fallback is a deterministic practice marker; pair it with the lesson’s specific inspection task. For commands that edit files, manage services, change network/firewall state, partition disks, change permissions recursively, or alter boot settings, use an isolated VM, take a snapshot/backup, review the exact target, and prepare a recovery path before acting.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the command is missing, check whether the required package is installed and which distribution you are using. If access is denied, do not immediately escalate to root; confirm the target path, identity, and required permission. If the result differs, capture the command, output, version, and environment so the issue can be reproduced.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember the core relationship: Linux access decisions combine identity, ownership, mode bits, optional ACLs, and higher-level security policy. Apply least privilege. The goal is to explain the observed result, test a boundary case, and record a limitation rather than memorize a command in isolation.
